newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: OLYMPICS-NEW CHIEF FOR SYDNEY 2000 GAMES.
newsitem.headline: OLYMPICS-NEW CHIEF FOR SYDNEY 2000 GAMES.

text.p: Sydney's 2000 Olympics organising committee appointed a former prime ministerial advisor as chief executive on Thursday in its third major managerial upheaval in a year.
The latest change at the top occurred only weeks after the International Olympic Committee (IOC) stressed the need for stability during preparations for the Games.

In a separate development on Thursday, the private consortium building the A$660 million (US$515 million) Olympic stadium was facing a huge flop in its bid to fund half the construction costs through a public share offer.
As a result, financial underwriters for the project would be liable for a predicted shortfall of up to A$240 million (US$188 million) in the costs of building the 110,000-seater venue.

On an eventful day for Sydney's Olympic organisers, Sandy Hollway, a career bureaucrat and diplomat who previously worked for former Labor Prime Minister Bob Hawke, was appointed chief executive after the sudden resignation of Mal Hemmerling.
The Sydney Olympic Committee for the Olympic Games (SOCOG) has been plagued by the loss of senior personnel during the past year.

During that period, two businessmen have resigned from the position as SOCOG president, leaving local politician Michael Knight to fill the role. A host of senior executives have also left the organising body.
Speaking at a hastily-arranged news conference, Hemmerling, who previously ran the Formula One grand prix in Adelaide for 10 years, said he made his decision to resign earlier this week.

"I leave now at a time when the organisation is in great shape. Left any later, it would not have been to the advantage of SOCOG," said Hemmerling, who will receive 12 months' salary in a golden handshake worth a reported A$500,000 (US$392,000).
But according to local media, Knight had forced Hemmerling's resignation because of personality differences between the pair.
Knight also holds the portfolio of Minister for the Olympics in the Labor-controlled New South Wales state government, which is underwriting the infrastructure costs of staging the Games.
"There is no instability in the (SOCOG) board. The board is very united," Knight said.
IOC officials, determined to avoid the troubles that beset last year's Olympic Games in Atlanta, have previously stated the need for continuity in decision making within SOCOG.
Knight said the IOC had been informed of Hemmerling's resignation over the past two days.

IOC Co-ordination Commissioner for the Sydney Olympics Jacques Rogge, the man responsible for monitoring the city's progress before the Games, cautioned SOCOG on the issue, according to Thursday's Sydney Morning Herald newspaper.

Speaking at IOC headquarters in Lausanne several weeks ago, Rogge said: "We plead for stability now in all aspects of the Olympic Games. ..I don't think SOCOG can afford too many changes in the key positions now," the paper reported.
Hollway, who was Hawke's chief of staff at Federal parliament in Canberra between 1988 and 1990, joined the 15-member SOCOG board as deputy chief executive four months ago.
